technical.prompt: What is distressed investing?
expectedPoints: Buying the debt or equity of companies in or near financial distress
Securities usually trade at deep discounts
Returns come from recoveries, restructurings or turnarounds

choices.answer: Buying securities of troubled companies at deep discounts
distractors: Investing only in fast-growing start-ups
Buying government bonds during recessions
Lending to companies with top credit ratings

technical.prompt: What does loan-to-own mean?
expectedPoints: Buying a company's debt with the aim of ending up owning it
Usually targets the class expected to receive equity in a restructuring
Debt is converted into equity through the process
Can be a cheaper route to control

choices.answer: Buying debt with the aim of converting it into ownership
distractors: Lending money only to companies you already own
Borrowing to buy a company's shares
Leasing assets to a company you control

technical.prompt: What is special situations investing?
expectedPoints: Investing around unusual events or complex situations
Examples include restructurings, spin-offs, litigation or rescue financing
Returns depend on catalysts rather than market direction

choices.answer: Investing around unusual events using flexible structures
distractors: Investing only in companies with special dividends
Investing only in regulated industries
Buying index funds during special market days

technical.prompt: Why does the debt of a distressed company trade well below face value?
expectedPoints: Risk of default and partial recovery
Many investors are forced or choose to sell
The market price reflects expected recovery and risk

choices.answer: Investors expect only partial recovery and demand a return for risk
distractors: Interest rates on the debt have been cut to zero
The debt no longer has any legal claim
Face value is reduced by regulators

technical.prompt: What is a blocking position in a class of claims?
expectedPoints: Holding enough of a class to stop it accepting a plan
In a typical court process, more than one third of the amount voting
A common goal of distressed investors

choices.answer: Enough of a class's claims to stop it accepting a plan
distractors: A position that cannot be sold for a set period
A short position in a company's shares
A loan that blocks new borrowing

technical.prompt: What is an ad hoc creditor group?
expectedPoints: An informal group of holders of the same debt
Usually unofficial, unlike a court-appointed committee

choices.answer: An informal group of creditors negotiating together
distractors: A committee appointed by the court
A group of shareholders electing a board
The company's internal treasury team

technical.prompt: What is rescue financing?
expectedPoints: New capital provided to a company facing a liquidity crisis
Often expensive, with high interest, fees or warrants

choices.answer: Costly new capital that helps a struggling company survive
distractors: A government grant for failed companies
A refund of taxes paid in good years
Low-cost debt for top-rated companies

technical.prompt: What is structured equity?
expectedPoints: Equity with special protections or terms
Examples include preferred returns, liquidation preferences or conversion rights
Gives downside protection with upside participation
Used when plain equity or debt doesn't fit

choices.answer: Equity with protections such as preferences or conversion
distractors: Common stock that carries no special rights
A loan that pays no interest at all
Shares that only employees are allowed to hold

technical.prompt: What is a private investment in public equity?
expectedPoints: A private placement of shares or securities in a listed company
Sold directly to one or a few investors
Often at a discount or with added terms
A fast way to raise capital

choices.answer: A direct private sale of a listed company's securities
distractors: An IPO sold only to retail investors
A public offering of private company bonds
A buyback of shares from private holders

technical.prompt: What is claims trading in a bankruptcy?
expectedPoints: Buying and selling claims against a bankrupt company
Includes bank debt, bonds and supplier claims

choices.answer: Buying and selling claims against a bankrupt company
distractors: Trading insurance claims between insurers
Selling the company's shares on an exchange
Transferring employee pension rights

technical.prompt: How do going-concern value and liquidation value differ for a distressed company?
expectedPoints: Going-concern value assumes the business keeps operating
Liquidation value assumes assets are sold off
The comparison guides reorganisation versus liquidation

choices.answer: Value if it keeps operating versus value if its assets are sold
distractors: Book value versus market value of shares
Value before tax versus value after tax
Value in one country versus another

technical.prompt: What does it mean for a class of claims to be out of the money?
expectedPoints: The company's value doesn't reach that class
It is expected to recover little or nothing
Classes above it absorb all the value
Its holders often receive only small settlements

choices.answer: The company's value does not reach that class
distractors: The class has been fully repaid
The class holds only cash
The class ranks first in priority

technical.prompt: Why do distressed investors study credit documents so carefully?
expectedPoints: They define rights, priority and collateral
Show what the company is allowed to do
Small wording differences can change recoveries

choices.answer: Wording defines rights and can change recoveries
distractors: Documents set the market price of the debt
Regulators require investors to sign them
They list every creditor's phone number

technical.prompt: What is post-reorganisation equity?
expectedPoints: Shares in the company after it emerges from restructuring
Usually given to creditors in exchange for their claims
Can offer upside as the company recovers

choices.answer: Shares in the company after it emerges from restructuring
distractors: Shares held by old owners before the restructuring
Debt issued to repay creditors
Equity in the company's bank

technical.prompt: What is an operational turnaround?
expectedPoints: Fixing the business itself, not just its balance sheet
Cost cuts, pricing changes and exiting losing lines
Needed when problems go beyond excess debt

choices.answer: Fixing the business itself, beyond the balance sheet
distractors: Changing the company's legal name
Moving the stock listing
Refinancing debt at a lower rate only

technical.prompt: What are the main risks of distressed investing?
expectedPoints: Recoveries may be lower than expected
Processes can take longer than planned

technical.prompt: What is a catalyst in special situations investing?
expectedPoints: An event expected to unlock value

choices.answer: An event expected to unlock value
distractors: The investor's minimum return target
A fee paid to advisers
The company's largest customer

technical.prompt: Why do many distressed investors focus on senior secured debt?
expectedPoints: Highest priority and backed by collateral
Often the fulcrum in deep distress

choices.answer: It has the highest priority and collateral behind it
distractors: It always pays the highest coupon
It is never affected by bankruptcy
It gives voting rights at shareholder meetings

technical.prompt: What is a liquidation preference on preferred equity?

distractors: A penalty paid if the company liquidates
A right to force the company into liquidation
The price at which common shares are issued
